Electrostatic field lines **begin on positive charges and end on negative ones** - they
never close on themselves.
**Step 1 — test the statement about closed loops.** An electrostatic field is
**conservative**:
∮ Ē·d̄l̄ = **0** ✓
If a field line formed a closed loop, one could carry a charge round it and gain energy
each circuit, since the force would always have a component along the motion ✓ That is a
perpetual-motion machine, so the statement is **false** - and it is the one to pick.
**Step 2 — check the other three.**
"**the tangent to a line of force gives the direction of E**" ✓ **true** - that is the
definition of a field line.
"**a negative test charge feels a force opposite to the field**" ✓ **true** - F̄ = qĒ,
and a negative q reverses the direction.
"**field lines never intersect**" ✓ **true** - at a crossing point the field would have
two directions at once, which is impossible.
**Where field lines do begin and end.** On **charges** ✓ outward from positive, inward to
negative. If there is net charge in a region, some lines are unterminated within it and
run off to infinity.
**The contrast with magnetic field lines.** Those **always** form closed loops, because
∇·B̄ = 0 and no magnetic monopoles exist ✓ There is nowhere for a magnetic field line to
start or stop - a fundamental difference between the two fields, and the source of the
confusion this question probes.
**The one case where electric field lines do close.** An **induced** electric field,
produced by a changing magnetic flux, has
∮ Ē·d̄l̄ = −dΦ/dt ≠ 0 ✓
and its lines **do** form closed loops - which is how a transformer and a betatron work.
But that field is not **electrostatic**, and no potential can be defined for it.
**Why lines cannot cross, more carefully.** The field at a point is a single vector with
one direction ✓ Two lines through the same point would assign two directions to it. The
only exception is a **null point**, where E = 0 and no line is defined at all.
∴ the statement that electric field lines form closed loops.

Compute the dipole moment as the **vector sum** of the individual charge-position
products.
**Step 1 — choose a convenient origin.** Put it at **C**, where the −4q sits ✓ Then that
charge contributes nothing, since its position vector is zero.
**Step 2 — write the two remaining contributions.**
p̄ = 2q r̄_A + 2q r̄_B
where r̄_A and r̄_B both have magnitude **x**, being sides of the equilateral triangle
from C ✓
**Step 3 — add the two vectors.** The angle between them is the triangle's interior
angle at C, **60°**:
|r̄_A + r̄_B| = 2x cos(60°/2)
= 2x cos 30°
= **x√3** ✓
**Step 4 — multiply by the charge.**
|p̄| = 2q(x√3)
= **2√3 qx** ✓
**Why the origin may be chosen freely.** The total charge is
2q + 2q − 4q = **0** ✓
For a system of **zero net charge** the dipole moment is independent of the origin -
which is why putting it at C, the simplest choice, is legitimate.
**A check with a different origin.** Put the origin at the midpoint of AB. Then A and B
are at ±(x/2) along AB, and C is at distance x√3/2 perpendicular to it:
contributions from A and B: 2q(x/2) − 2q(x/2) = **0** along AB ✓
contribution from C: −4q x (x√3/2) = **−2√3 qx** perpendicular
magnitude **2√3 qx** ✓ the same answer, confirming the origin-independence.
**The direction of the moment.** From the negative charge towards the positive ones -
here from C towards the midpoint of AB ✓ The system behaves as a single dipole of
charge 4q separated by the distance from C to that midpoint, x√3/2:
p = 4q x (√3x/2) = **2√3 qx** ✓ a third route to the same result.
**Why the law of cosines rather than simple addition.** The two vectors are at 60°, not
parallel ✓ Adding their magnitudes would give 4qx, which is one of the errors the
distractors are built on.
**Reading the distractors.** **2qx** ✗ counts only one charge. **3qx** ✗ and **3√2 qx**
✗ follow from using the wrong angle - 90° would give 2√2 qx, and 120° would give 2qx ✓
∴ 2√3 qx.

Removing electrons leaves the sphere **positively** charged; outside it, the field is
that of a point charge at the centre.
**Step 1 — find the charge on the sphere.**
Q = ne
= (4 x 10¹⁰)(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹)
= **6·4 x 10⁻⁹ C** ✓ positive, since electrons have been removed.
**Step 2 — check that the point lies outside.** The sphere's **diameter** is 20 cm, so
its **radius** is **10 cm** ✓ The point at 20 cm from the centre is therefore well
outside, and the point-charge formula applies.
**Step 3 — apply the formula.**
E = kQ/r²
= (9 x 10⁹)(6·4 x 10⁻⁹)/(0·20)²
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
numerator: 9 x 6·4 = **57·6**
denominator: (0·2)² = **0·04**
E = 57·6/0·04
= **1440 N C⁻¹** ✓
**The trap in the question.** It gives the **diameter**, not the radius ✓ Taking 20 cm
as the radius would put the point **on** the surface, and a careless reading can lead to
the wrong formula altogether.
**Why outside a sphere behaves like a point charge.** By **Gauss's law**, a spherically
symmetric distribution produces outside itself exactly the field of all its charge
concentrated at the centre ✓ The result is exact, not an approximation.
**The field at the surface, for comparison.** At r = 0·10 m:
E = 57·6/0·01 = **5760 N C⁻¹** ✓
four times the value at 20 cm, as the inverse square requires - and that 5760 is
offered as the first distractor, for anyone who confuses radius with diameter.
**The field inside the conductor.** **Zero** ✓ all the excess charge resides on the
surface and the interior is completely shielded.
**Reading the remaining distractors.** **640 N C⁻¹** ✗ would need r = 0·3 m. **Zero** ✗
is the value **inside** the conductor, not at 20 cm from the centre ✓ Checking whether
the point is inside or outside is the first step in every problem of this kind.
∴ 1440.

Whether a magnetic field is seen depends on whether the charge is **moving relative to
the observer**.
**Step 1 — take the passenger's view.** Passenger A travels **with** the train, so the
charge is **at rest** in A's frame ✓ A stationary charge produces an **electric field
only** - there is no current and hence no magnetic field.
**Step 2 — take the ground observer's view.** To B on the ground the charge is
**moving**, at the train's speed ✓ A moving charge constitutes a current, so B detects
**both** an electric field and a **magnetic** field.
**Step 3 — conclude.** **B observes both electric and magnetic fields** ✓
**Why this is not a paradox.** Electric and magnetic fields are **not separate
absolutes**; they are two aspects of a single **electromagnetic field**, and how it
divides between them depends on the observer's motion ✓ What one observer calls a pure
electric field, another, moving relative to the first, sees as a mixture of electric and
magnetic.
**The transformation, for a slow train.**
B̄′ ≈ −(v̄ x Ē)/c² ✓
so the magnetic field B sees is extremely small - of order v/c² times the electric
field - but it is genuinely there.
**What both observers agree on.** The **physical outcome** of any experiment ✓ If a test
charge is deflected, both see the same deflection; they merely attribute it to
differently apportioned electric and magnetic forces. That invariance of the physics,
with the fields themselves frame-dependent, is one of the roots of special relativity.
**The historical importance.** Einstein's 1905 paper opens with exactly this kind of
puzzle - a magnet and a conductor in relative motion - and notes that the **observable**
current is the same whichever is said to be moving, though the conventional explanation
differs ✓ The resolution was relativity.
**Reading the distractors.** "**A observes both**" ✗ - the charge is at rest for A, so
there is no magnetic field in that frame. "**A observes only magnetic**" ✗ - a charge
always produces an electric field. "**B observes only electric**" ✗ - B sees the charge
moving, so a magnetic field is unavoidable ✓
∴ B observes both electric and magnetic fields.

The peak emf of a rotating coil is **NBAω**.
**Step 1 — convert the area to SI units.**
A = 25 cm x 10 cm
= 0·25 m x 0·10 m
= **0·025 m²** ✓
**Step 2 — find the angular frequency.** The coil turns at 50 cycles per second:
ω = 2πf
= 2π(50)
= **100π rad s⁻¹**
**Step 3 — apply the formula.**
e₀ = NBAω
= (300)(4 x 10⁻²)(0·025)(100π)
**Step 4 — multiply step by step.**
300 x 4 x 10⁻² = **12**
12 x 0·025 = **0·3**
0·3 x 100π = **30π volt** ✓
**Where the formula comes from.** The flux through the coil is
Φ = NBA cos ωt ✓
and by Faraday's law
e = −dΦ/dt = NBAω sin ωt ✓
so the emf varies sinusoidally with peak value **NBAω** - this is the elementary a.c.
generator.
**When the emf is greatest.** At the instant the coil's **plane contains** the field,
so that the flux through it is momentarily **zero** but changing fastest ✓ A quarter
turn later the flux is maximum and the emf is **zero** - the two are 90° out of step.
**The numerical value.** 30π = **94·2 V** ✓ a realistic output for a coil of these
dimensions spinning at 3000 rpm.
**Why each factor helps.** More turns, a stronger field, a larger area and a faster
rotation all raise the emf in direct proportion ✓ Real generators increase every one of
them, and use an iron core to raise B further.
**Checking the units.**
[NBAω] = (T)(m²)(s⁻¹) = (Wb)(s⁻¹) = **V** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **3π** ✗ is a factor of ten out, from taking the area as
0·0025 m². **300π** ✗ and **3000π** ✗ come from leaving the dimensions in centimetres ✓
Converting cm to m at the start avoids all three.
∴ 30 π.
